script.opening: (Brisk, matter-of-fact, glasses on; daughter heard in the background.) "I've noticed over the last few weeks that the middle of my sight in my left eye has gone blurry, and — this is odd — straight lines like the door frame and the lines on my crossword look wavy and bent. I can still see round the edges. I assume it's just old age and there's nothing to be done, but my daughter nagged me to get it checked."

facts.text: "A few weeks ago. It seems worse this week." About 3 weeks; noticeably worse over the last 5 days.

If asked to look at a door frame or grid with each eye: "With the left it's bent in the middle and a bit smudged. The right looks straight." "More smudged than dark. No pain." No flashes or floaters, no red eye.
"The crossword's hard. Faces across the room are fuzzy." Struggling with the cooker dials. No falls yet.
If asked: "Not yet" — she doesn't drive any more (stopped 2 years ago).
"My mother. They just said her eyes went."
"More than I should" — 15 a day for 60 years. "I've tried before. I might try again, for my eyes."
Hypertension (ramipril), osteoarthritis. No diabetes. No allergies. Last optician visit 3 years ago. Takes no supplements.
If asked about seeing things that aren't there: no.
Widowed, lives alone in a bungalow; daughter visits twice a week. Loves crosswords and her church choir.

Stoical and a bit fatalistic. If asked what worries her: "I don't want to end up like my mother. She couldn't do anything for herself at the end." Surprised by treatment: "So it is old age?" then "Injections in the eye? Goodness." Lukewarm but open on smoking. If told it's age and nothing can be done, accepts sadly (the trap).

ice.ideas: "It's just old age — nothing can be done."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear of going blind and losing her independence like her mother; losing her crosswords and choir.

cues: "Straight lines look wavy." — metamorphopsia; ask how fast it came on.
"It seems worse this week." — recent change suggests wet AMD.
"I don't want to end up like my mother." — the fear, if invited.

checkpoints.text: Recognises AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION from central vision loss + METAMORPHOPSIA (wavy/distorted lines) with preserved peripheral vision in an older adult — not accepting "just old age"

Makes the critical DRY vs WET distinction — recognising recent, rapidly progressive distortion/central loss as possible WET AMD needing URGENT referral to a macula service, normally within 1 working day (NICE NG82 — urgent, not an emergency; treatment within 14 days, NICE QS180), for sight-saving anti-VEGF

Takes a targeted history (speed of onset, which eye, functional impact, Amsler-grid distortion) and assesses risk (smoking, family history), knowing acuity cannot be measured reliably on video and must not delay referral

Addresses modifiable risk — SMOKING cessation (major modifiable factor; NICE NG209), cardiovascular health, and does NOT recommend supplements (NG82 research recommendation only; beta-carotene harmful in smokers) — and optimises other eye health (cataract/refraction)

Refers appropriately — urgently if wet-AMD features, routinely for slow dry AMD — and gives safety-netting to detect conversion to wet AMD (Amsler grid as a prompt, with its low sensitivity explained)
Counters the "just old age, nothing can be done" fatalism honestly — wet AMD is treatable, aids/support help dry AMD — without overpromising

Takes the FUNCTIONAL/EMOTIONAL impact seriously (reading, faces, independence, driving/DVLA, falls/isolation, fear of blindness, Charles Bonnet syndrome, certification of visual impairment), validates the daughter’s prompt, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: appropriate-urgency referral, Amsler-grid monitoring and what change warrants urgent review, smoking-cessation and low-vision support, DVLA/driving advice, and review — active management, not fatalistic dismissal

worked.txt: "Your daughter was right to send you. The blur in the centre with straight lines looking wavy is a specific condition — age-related macular degeneration — not just ‘getting old’, and crucially what we do next depends on which type it is."

"How quickly did the wavy distortion come on — over a few weeks, or has it changed fast in the last days? … That matters a lot: a sudden, recent change can mean the treatable ‘wet’ type, where prompt injections can save sight. A slow blur is usually the ‘dry’ type."

"Because your distortion is fairly recent, I’m referring you urgently to the macular clinic — they normally see people within a working day — so they can check for the treatable type. If it’s the slower dry type, they’ll confirm it and set up support."

"There’s genuinely a lot we can do: if it’s wet, injections; either way, stopping smoking is the single biggest thing for your eyes — and please avoid eye vitamins containing beta-carotene, which aren’t safe for smokers — and there are magnifiers and low-vision aids that make a real difference to reading."

"This affects reading, recognising faces, maybe driving — that’s a big deal, not trivial. We’ll sort support, and I’ll be honest about driving and the DVLA. Some people with this see things that aren’t there — patterns or faces — and that’s a known effect called Charles Bonnet syndrome, not a sign of losing your mind. How are you feeling about it all?"

"I’ll give you an Amsler grid — a little square of lines to check each eye daily. If the lines suddenly look more wavy or a dark patch appears, that’s a sign to be seen urgently — though the grid can miss changes, so tell us about any new blur too. And we’ll review you after the clinic."

f.learning: Gradual loss of CENTRAL vision with METAMORPHOPSIA (straight lines appearing wavy/distorted) and difficulty reading/recognising faces, with PRESERVED peripheral vision, in an older adult is the hallmark of AGE-RELATED MACULAR DEGENERATION (AMD) — recognise the pattern rather than accept "just old age". The critical distinction is DRY AMD (gradual over months/years; no specific cure — managed with visual aids, support and risk modification; NICE NG82 makes only a research recommendation on supplements, and beta-carotene formulas are unsafe in smokers) versus WET (neovascular) AMD, which causes RAPID, recent distortion/central loss and is a TIME-SENSITIVE URGENT referral to a macula service, normally within 1 working day (NICE NG82, 2018 — urgent, not an emergency), with diagnosis and treatment within 14 days (NICE QS180), because prompt anti-VEGF injections (NICE TA1022 and earlier appraisals) can preserve sight — so recent, rapidly progressive distortion must be treated as possible wet AMD and referred urgently. Take a targeted history (speed of onset, which eye, functional impact, Amsler-grid distortion — a low-sensitivity prompt), leave acuity to the macula service rather than trying to measure it on video, and address modifiable risk — SMOKING cessation is the major modifiable factor (NICE NG209), with general cardiovascular health — optimising other eye health. Refer urgently for wet-AMD features and routinely for slow dry AMD, with safety-netting for new distortion or blur to detect conversion to wet AMD (the Amsler grid helps but can miss change). Crucially, counter the "it’s just old age, nothing can be done" fatalism: wet AMD is treatable and even dry AMD benefits from aids, support and risk modification; and take the functional and emotional impact seriously — loss of reading, faces, independence and driving (DVLA implications), with falls and isolation risk — involving low-vision support, certification of visual impairment and information about Charles Bonnet syndrome (NICE NG82; QS180).

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG82 Age-related macular degeneration (2018) · [2] NICE QS180 Serious eye disorders (2019) · [3] NICE TA1022 and related anti-VEGF technology appraisals (TA155, TA294, TA672, TA800) · [4] NICE NG209 Tobacco: preventing uptake, promoting quitting and treating dependence (2021, updated) · [5] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: visual disorders
knowledge.summary: New central blur with distortion over a few weeks in a 78-year-old smoker is possible wet AMD. NICE NG82 wants an urgent referral to a macula service, normally within 1 working day, because prompt anti-VEGF treatment can preserve sight. It is not “just old age”.

points.t: Central blur, straight lines looking wavy (metamorphopsia), difficulty reading or recognising faces, with peripheral vision preserved. Age, smoking and family history are the established risk factors.

Late AMD may be wet (neovascular) or dry (geographic atrophy). New or rapidly worsening distortion or central loss suggests wet active disease. Slow change over months or years suggests dry disease. Only macular imaging (OCT) can tell them apart, so the history decides the urgency, not the diagnosis.

NICE NG82 [1]: refer people with suspected late AMD (wet active) urgently to a macula service, normally within 1 working day, whether or not vision is affected. It is urgent, not an emergency. NG82 [1] and QS180 [2]: diagnose and treat within 14 days of referral.

Anti-VEGF intravitreal injections for wet active AMD, within the acuity and lesion criteria set in NICE TA1022 and the earlier appraisals [3]. There is no treatment that reverses dry AMD; care focuses on low-vision support and monitoring.

Smoking is the main modifiable risk. Offer stop-smoking support (NICE NG209 [4]). Supplements: NG82 makes only a research recommendation. Beta-carotene-containing formulas raise lung cancer risk in smokers, so do not suggest them.

NG82 [1]: give information on the condition, low-vision services, certification of visual impairment, and Charles Bonnet syndrome (visual hallucinations that are not a sign of mental illness). QS180 [2]: offer certification as soon as eligible.

DVLA [5] Group 1: read a number plate at 20 metres, 6/12 with both eyes open, and meet the field standard. Tell DVLA if both eyes (or the only eye) are affected, or if told the standard may not be met.

Onset and recent change, each-eye line test on video, scotoma, pain or flashes; recognised that OCT at a macula service decides the type.
Wet versus dry AMD; other causes of central loss (macular hole, vein occlusion, cataract) considered.
Recognised recent, progressing distortion as possible wet AMD needing urgent referral; asked about falls.
Named AMD, explained wet and dry, and that peripheral vision is spared.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Falls risk, low-vision support, certification and Charles Bonnet information planned; daughter involved with consent.
Daily each-eye check, same-day contact for sudden change or the other eye, follow-up call in a week.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options

Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Idea (old age, nothing to be done), concern (ending up dependent like her mother), expectation (to be told it’s age).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

model.text: Hello Mrs Whitlock, it’s Dr Evans. Thanks for joining the video call. What’s been happening with your eyes?

Over the last few weeks the middle of my sight in my left eye has gone blurry, and straight lines like the door frame and the lines on my crossword look wavy and bent. I can still see round the edges. I assume it’s just old age and nothing can be done, but my daughter nagged me to get it checked.

Your daughter was right to send you, and I’m glad you came. I’d like to ask some questions and then explain what I think, because what you describe is a specific problem, not simply old age. Is that alright?
model.why: Validates the daughter’s prompt and sets an agenda

model.text: Go on then.
When did you first notice the wavy lines, and has it changed over the last few days?
model.why: Establishes speed of onset, key to wet AMD

model.text: A few weeks ago. It seems worse this week.
Could you cover your right eye and look at the door frame behind you? Then cover the left and do the same.
With the left it’s bent in the middle and a bit smudged. The right looks straight.
Thank you. Is there a dark or empty patch in the centre? Any pain, redness, flashes or a curtain?
model.why: Checks for scotoma and excludes other causes

model.text: More smudged than dark. No pain.
How is it affecting you day to day: reading, faces, the television, getting about?
The crossword’s hard. Faces across the room are fuzzy.
Have you had any falls or near misses, particularly on stairs or kerbs?
Not yet.
You mentioned family going blind in old age. Do you know what it was?
My mother. They just said her eyes went.
And you still smoke. How much at the moment?
More than I should.
You said it’s just old age. Is there something about it that worries you?
I don’t want to end up like my mother. She couldn’t do anything for herself at the end.
That’s a real fear, especially having seen it happen. Thank you for telling me.
model.why: Acknowledges fear of blindness and dependence

model.text: What you describe sounds like age-related macular degeneration, which affects the macula, the part of the eye for detailed central vision. It doesn’t affect the side vision, so it doesn’t cause total blindness.
model.why: Names AMD and corrects the fear of total blindness

model.text: So it is old age?

Age is part of it, but there are two types, and it matters which. The ‘wet’ type can come on over weeks, like yours, and it can be treated with injections into the eye that can stop it getting worse. That treatment works best if it starts soon.
model.why: Explains the wet-dry distinction and why speed matters

model.text: Injections in the eye? Goodness.
It sounds worse than it is: the eye is numbed first. The specialists will explain it fully. The main thing is that ‘nothing can be done’ isn’t true here.
I’m going to refer you urgently to the macula clinic today. They aim to see and, if needed, treat people within two weeks. They’ll scan the back of your eye to tell which type it is.
Smoking is the biggest thing you can change for your eyes. Would you be open to some help to cut down or stop?
I’ve tried before. I might try again, for my eyes.
That’s great. I’ll put you in touch with the stop-smoking service. Please don’t buy eye vitamins in the meantime, because some types aren’t safe for smokers.
model.why: Warns against beta-carotene supplements in smokers

model.text: And if you drive, please don’t while the left eye is like this until you’ve been checked, and we’ll go through the DVLA rules once we know more.
I’ll bear that in mind.

Check each eye on a straight line every day. If the distortion suddenly gets worse, a dark patch appears, or the other eye starts to change, ring us or the clinic the same day. Can you tell me the plan back?
Urgent eye clinic, check the lines each day, ring if worse, and think about stopping smoking.
That’s it. I’ll call you in a week to make sure the appointment has come through, and we can talk about low-vision support and what your daughter can help with.

social.t: Central vision loss affects reading, faces, medication labels and stairs. Consider a falls and home-safety review and involve her daughter with consent.
Her mother’s experience shapes her fear. Explain that AMD spares side vision, and point to low-vision services.

legal.t: Group 1: tell DVLA if both eyes (or the only eye) are affected, or if told the visual standard may not be met; drivers must read a number plate at 20 metres (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
The eye clinic can certify sight impairment (CVI) once eligible, which opens access to social care support (NICE QS180).

professional.t: Acuity cannot be measured reliably on video; refer on the history and let the macula service measure it.
Use the local urgent macula pathway; NG82 says urgent, normally within 1 working day, and not an emergency referral.

community.t: The Macular Society and RNIB offer information, peer support and advice on low-vision aids. Local stop-smoking services support quitting.

redFlags: New or rapidly worsening distortion or central blur (possible wet AMD)
Sudden change in the other eye
Pain, redness, flashes or a curtain (a different diagnosis)
psychosocial: Her mother’s sight loss and fear of dependence
ice: Idea: “It’s just old age; nothing can be done.”
Concern: ending up dependent like her mother
Expectation: to be told it is age

playbook.diagnosis: “This sounds like age-related macular degeneration. Because it has come on over a few weeks, it could be the wet type, which can be treated, so it needs an urgent specialist check.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The macula is the centre of the camera film at the back of the eye, the part you read with. When it’s damaged, the middle of the picture blurs and bends, but the edges stay.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought nothing could be done, and you’re worried about ending up like your mother. There is a treatable type, and side vision isn’t affected.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter with consent, plan low-vision support and a falls review, and follow up the referral.
sharedPlan: Urgent referral to the macula service (NG82: normally within 1 working day)
No driving until checked; DVLA advice after diagnosis

safetyNet: Daily each-eye check on a straight line
Same-day contact for sudden worsening, a dark patch, or change in the other eye
Practice call in a week to confirm the appointment

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by agreeing with the patient. She tells you it is old age; the marks go to the candidate who identifies possible wet AMD, refers with the right urgency, and takes her fear seriously.

items.why: Recent distortion suggests wet AMD, which is treatable if caught early.
items.fix: Name AMD and explain the treatable type.

items.fail: Not asking how quickly it came on.
items.why: Speed of onset sets the urgency.
items.fix: “When did it start, and has it changed in the last few days?”

items.fail: Referring routinely, or giving a vague urgency such as “within days”.
items.why: NICE NG82: urgent referral to a macula service, normally within 1 working day, for suspected wet active AMD.
items.fix: Refer urgently today via the local macula pathway.

items.fail: Recommending eye vitamins to a smoker.
items.why: NG82 has no practice recommendation on supplements, and beta-carotene raises lung cancer risk in smokers.

items.fail: Missing the fear rooted in her mother’s sight loss.
items.why: Her unspoken concern about dependence drives her fatalism.
items.fix: Ask what worries her and explain that side vision is spared.

items.why: Central loss affects safety at home and on the road.
items.fix: Advise no driving until assessed; explain the DVLA rules; consider falls.

items.fail: No safety-net for the other eye.
items.why: The fellow eye is at risk and change there also needs rapid review.
items.fix: Daily each-eye check; same-day contact for new change.

timeMap.d: Let her finish; validate the daughter’s prompt.
Onset and recent change, each-eye line test on camera, dark patch, pain or flashes, reading and faces, falls, family history, smoking.
“Just old age”, fear of ending up like her mother.
AMD, central not total loss, wet vs dry, why weeks of change matters.
Urgent macula referral, stop-smoking support, no beta-carotene supplements, driving, daily check, follow-up call and support.

wordPics.fail: Agrees it is old age; suggests the optician when convenient; no question about speed of onset; no smoking advice; ignores the fear of blindness.
wordPics.pass: Recognises AMD, identifies recent onset as possible wet AMD, refers urgently to a macula service, advises on smoking, and safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: uses the camera for a simple each-eye check; explains that side vision is spared; counters the fatalism without overpromising; explores the fear rooted in her mother’s experience; warns against beta-carotene in a smoker; plans low-vision support, Charles Bonnet information and driving advice; follows up the referral.

avoid.dont: “It’s your age, I’m afraid. There isn’t much we can do.”
avoid.instead: “This sounds like macular degeneration. One type can be treated, and it needs checking urgently.”
avoid.why: Wet AMD is treatable; fatalism delays sight-saving treatment.

avoid.dont: “Get your optician to look at it when you can.”
avoid.instead: “I’m referring you urgently to the macula clinic today.”
avoid.why: NICE NG82: urgent referral to a macula service for suspected wet active AMD.

avoid.instead: “Stopping smoking is the best thing for your eyes; please don’t buy eye vitamins, as some aren’t safe for smokers.”
avoid.why: NG82 makes no practice recommendation on supplements, and beta-carotene raises lung cancer risk in smokers.

DVLA [5] Group 1: read a number plate at 20 metres, 6/12 with both eyes open, and meet the field standard. Tell DVLA if both eyes (or the only eye) are affected, or if told the standard may not be met.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Let her describe the blur and wavy lines; acknowledged the daughter’s prompt.
Reading, faces, falls, independence and support at home; smoking.
Picked up “worse this week”, the mother’s sight loss and the fatalism.
Idea (old age, nothing to be done), concern (ending up dependent like her mother), expectation (to be told it’s age).
Onset and recent change, each-eye line test on video, scotoma, pain or flashes; recognised that OCT at a macula service decides the type.
Wet versus dry AMD; other causes of central loss (macular hole, vein occlusion, cataract) considered.
Recognised recent, progressing distortion as possible wet AMD needing urgent referral; asked about falls.
Named AMD, explained wet and dry, and that peripheral vision is spared.
Urgent macula referral (NG82: normally within 1 working day); stop-smoking support; no beta-carotene supplements; driving advice.
Falls risk, low-vision support, certification and Charles Bonnet information planned; daughter involved with consent.
Daily each-eye check, same-day contact for sudden change or the other eye, follow-up call in a week.

social.t: Central vision loss affects reading, faces, medication labels and stairs. Consider a falls and home-safety review and involve her daughter with consent.
Her mother’s experience shapes her fear. Explain that AMD spares side vision, and point to low-vision services.

legal.t: Group 1: tell DVLA if both eyes (or the only eye) are affected, or if told the visual standard may not be met; drivers must read a number plate at 20 metres (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).
The eye clinic can certify sight impairment (CVI) once eligible, which opens access to social care support (NICE QS180).

professional.t: Acuity cannot be measured reliably on video; refer on the history and let the macula service measure it.
Use the local urgent macula pathway; NG82 says urgent, normally within 1 working day, and not an emergency referral.

community.t: The Macular Society and RNIB offer information, peer support and advice on low-vision aids. Local stop-smoking services support quitting.

ice: Idea: “It’s just old age; nothing can be done.”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This sounds like age-related macular degeneration. Because it has come on over a few weeks, it could be the wet type, which can be treated, so it needs an urgent specialist check.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The macula is the centre of the camera film at the back of the eye, the part you read with. When it’s damaged, the middle of the picture blurs and bends, but the edges stay.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought nothing could be done, and you’re worried about ending up like your mother. There is a treatable type, and side vision isn’t affected.”
management.psychosocial: Involve her daughter with consent, plan low-vision support and a falls review, and follow up the referral.

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by agreeing with the patient. She tells you it is old age; the marks go to the candidate who identifies possible wet AMD, refers with the right urgency, and takes her fear seriously.

items.why: Recent distortion suggests wet AMD, which is treatable if caught early.
items.fix: Name AMD and explain the treatable type.

items.fail: Not asking how quickly it came on.
items.why: Speed of onset sets the urgency.
items.fix: “When did it start, and has it changed in the last few days?”

items.fail: Referring routinely, or giving a vague urgency such as “within days”.
items.why: NICE NG82: urgent referral to a macula service, normally within 1 working day, for suspected wet active AMD.
items.fix: Refer urgently today via the local macula pathway.

items.fail: Recommending eye vitamins to a smoker.
items.why: NG82 has no practice recommendation on supplements, and beta-carotene raises lung cancer risk in smokers.

items.fail: Missing the fear rooted in her mother’s sight loss.
items.why: Her unspoken concern about dependence drives her fatalism.
items.fix: Ask what worries her and explain that side vision is spared.

items.why: Central loss affects safety at home and on the road.
items.fix: Advise no driving until assessed; explain the DVLA rules; consider falls.

items.fail: No safety-net for the other eye.
items.why: The fellow eye is at risk and change there also needs rapid review.
items.fix: Daily each-eye check; same-day contact for new change.
